I have farmed these 20 mu in Quzhou for 45 years. After high school, I learned to pay attention to soil conditions and nutrient balance instead of just copying whatever my neighbors do. Last year my wheat made about 500 kg per mu and my maize about 580 kg. The soil here is loamy but I have noticed the eastern plots are getting lower in phosphorus, so I adjust my compound fertilizer there instead of spreading the same amount everywhere.

This October I will sow an improved wheat variety — I have used Jimai seeds for several years and they are reliable. I do rotary tillage before planting to break up the stubble and prepare a good seedbed. For fertilizer, I apply 18 kg nitrogen per mu in total: half as compound fertilizer at basal dressing, then I topdress with urea at the jointing stage when I can judge the crop condition with my own eyes. I also use 7 kg phosphorus and 5 kg potassium per mu. I irrigate four times from my well — before winter, at green-up, at jointing, and at grain filling. Some neighbors only water three times, but my well capacity is good and I would rather pay the pumping cost than risk yield loss. I spray pesticides four times on wheat: one herbicide after sowing, two insecticides for aphids and armyworm, and one fungicide at heading.

For summer maize, I plant right after wheat harvest in mid-June. The window is only a few days, so I use no-tillage direct seeding with a hired machine. I plant a hybrid maize — DengHai or Xianyu varieties work well here. Maize needs plenty of nitrogen but a bit less phosphorus than wheat, so I apply 16 kg nitrogen, 6 kg phosphorus, and 5 kg potassium per mu. Summer rainfall usually helps, but I keep my pump ready and will irrigate twice if July turns dry. Three pesticide applications are enough for maize: one herbicide at emergence, and two insecticides for corn borer.

My wife and I manage the farm alone now. Our son works off-farm in the city and sends some money home, which helps with input costs. But with 20 mu, I still hire machinery for tillage, seeding, and harvest — doing it all by hand is impossible at my age. I watch my budget closely: every bag of fertilizer and every hour of hired labor is real money out of my pocket. Still, I would rather apply a bit too much fertilizer than too little. A bad harvest at 68 years old would be a real disaster, but wasting a few kilograms of urea is just a cost I can absorb. I expect 520 kg per mu from wheat and 600 kg per mu from maize this year — solid numbers, not greedy.
